s: I only came here to show that I fully support the purpose of this meeting. I did not plan to speak. But since I have been asked, I cannot hold back. Out of love, I will say a few words.
One point has struck me in a special way. It is about our Lord Jesus, who is worthy of all worship, being our Head.
That blessed One wants His disciples to love one another. He wants them to be joined together in heart and in affection.

Without Him we would be lost forever. He poured out His life, even to death, so that we could live. He bent down so low that we could share His throne. So if this is what He wants—that we love one another and stand together as His disciples—shouldn't we obey Him out of love and thankfulness?
What are the biggest things that get in the way of love and unity among believers?

Being pleased with ourselves, thinking too highly of ourselves, pride, and thinking we know more than others. But suppose God's grace helps us overcome these evil habits. Suppose we learn to love our fellow believer and stand together with him. Then we may discover something. We may have more grace or knowledge than he does in one thing. But in four or five, or even ten things, he has more than we do.
Who am I to look down on my brother?
What do I have that I was not given?
Maybe I have more grace (though that is still open to question). If so, I received it from my Lord.
Maybe I have more knowledge (though that is also open to question). Do I owe it to my own mind?
Where does it come from?
If I know more than my fellow believer, it is because of God's grace.

So we are what we are because of God's grace. Every bit of power over sin, every bit of love for heavenly things, every desire to live by the Holy Scriptures, becomes ours only because God was pleased to bless us out of His rich grace. So who are we to look down on a brother just because a fellow disciple knows less or is spiritually weaker in some ways?
Jesus is our Head.
He wants us to love one another.
That blessed One gave His life so that I could be saved. So out of thankfulness to Him, let me obey. And if I find that pride is stopping me, let me ask for grace to overcome it.
“We who are strong should carry the weaknesses of the weak, and not please ourselves.”
When we meet a brother who is weak in grace or knowledge, our natural reaction is to say, “Oh, he is one of the weak ones.”
Our sinful human nature says, “Push him aside.”
But the Word of our blessed Lord says, “Carry the weaknesses of the weak.”
If I am strong, let me prove it. Let me put my shoulder under the load.
If I cannot be patient with my brother's weakness, that clearly shows that I am weak myself.
Why have we been given grace?
So that we can help our brother who is weaker or has been taught less. And so that by helping others we can bring glory to God.
I think it may be helpful to tell you about one thing from my own life.

Thirty-four years ago I began working in this country as a young servant of Christ, preaching the Word. I had just come to understand certain wonderful truths, such as the Lord's return and other things. My natural reaction was to look down on people who did not see those truths.
Thirty-four years have passed since then.
By God's grace I still hold on to those wonderful truths as firmly as ever. I defend them just as strongly. But the way I treat other disciples who disagree with me on these points is different now.
As a young servant of Christ, my attitude was, “Keep your distance!” I thought of them as people who had been taught very little.
What was the result?
Was it peace and joy in the Holy Spirit?
Was I copying the One who was patient with His disciples when they did not understand?
No. It was anything but copying Jesus. And the result was anything but peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
With God's help I now think differently, and I have for more than twenty years. Yet I have not given up the tiniest bit of the truths I received in 1829.

Now my goal is to be patient with people who may have been taught less. And as far as I am able to follow the example of my Lord, who is worthy of all worship, the result is peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
My dear fellow believers, I lovingly and earnestly beg you, especially the young ones, to think hard about this.
Pray that God will keep you from a proud spirit.
All that you have and all that you are comes from God's grace. That should make you gentle with your fellow disciples.
People often say that for the sake of peace and unity we should not be too fussy about certain parts of the truth. They say we should keep those parts quiet and treat them as if they do not matter.
I humbly say that I completely disagree with this. I do not think unity like that is real, or lasting, or based on the Bible.

If something is true, it is precious to the heart of Jesus. The blessed Spirit teaches it to us. It is found in God's book. So it is very valuable. We must treat it as worth guarding carefully and jealously.
So we are not free to treat the truth lightly, to value it less, or to push it into the background—much less to give it up—not even for the sake of unity.
We must buy the truth whatever it costs. But we should never sell it for any price, not even for our freedom or our life.

Yet while we hold on tightly to the truth—all the truth we believe the Holy Scriptures have taught us—we must always remember something. What should unite believers is not how much they know. It is the shared spiritual life they have in Jesus. They were bought by the blood of Jesus. They are members of the same family. They are going to the Father's house, and soon they will all be there. Because they share this one life, fellow believers should live together in unity.
The Father wants us to love one another. So does that blessed One who gave His life for us.
But someone may ask, “Is it really possible for believers who disagree on this and that to be united?”
Yes, it is. In the three orphan houses and six schools that I oversee, there are sixty teachers and other helpers.

Some of them belong to the Church of England. Others are Presbyterians, Independents, and Baptists, both those who hold to closed communion and those who hold to open communion. Others are Wesleyans from the Conference and from the Free Church groups, and some are from the so-called “Brethren.”
All of them come from different groups of believers. Yet they are united in this one goal of working for Christ.
We have been doing this work together for many years. In all that time I have never seen a quarrel break out because of these differences.
This is not because I think beliefs do not really matter. It is because I hold firmly to my own beliefs, but I have not demanded that these workers all think exactly the same.
When I take on helpers, one thing is essential: they must belong to Christ, the Head. They must hold on to the blessed Son of God.
Once that is settled, I never ask which church group they belong to.
I am not saying this to boast. I am saying it to praise God's grace.
People often say that the things preached from the platform can never actually be done in real life.

I insist that loving one another must be possible, because God commands it. And I especially want the dear brothers in Christ who have gathered these believers here in front of me to be sure of this: it is possible to do everything that is in line with God's will.
What God has commanded must be possible to do.
And let us not think that walking together in love is some extraordinary, advanced achievement for Christians.
Even the believers who have been taught the least should be willing to love, even if they do not agree on every point.
“Let us keep living by the same rule, as far as we have already come.”

We agree on many things. If we walk together like this, holding on in our hearts to Jesus as our Head, we will certainly grow. “And if you see anything differently, God will make even this clear to you.”
Don't say about anything, “I will never understand this.”
That is completely wrong.
When it comes to the things of God, never give up hope about anything.
Never make agreement on particular points of truth the basis for unity.
If my fellow believers disagree with me, I must not say, “It doesn't matter.” And I should not say, “I will never know this or that truth,” just because God may not have shown it to me yet.

Let there be more prayer, more study of God's Word, more humility, and more living out what we already know. In this way we will grow more united—not only in love, but also in the same mind and the same judgment.
In heaven there will be no differences.
There everyone is of one mind.
Let us aim for what heaven is like.
More patience and more faith will lead us further into blessing.
For Jesus' sake, may God give this to everyone gathered here!

Our salvation has two great purposes. The first and most important is that God may be glorified. The second, at the same time, is that His children may be made like His dear Son, to make sure that they will be happy forever.
They could never be happy, not even in heaven, unless they were made like Him in this way.
This work begins here, and it will be finished when we are with the Lord. Only then will we be made completely like Christ.

This is the wonderful, glorious hope of all who believe in the Lord Jesus. A day is coming when their will is completely swallowed up in God's will. They will have no will of their own. God will only need to show them His blessed will, and at once, deep in their souls, they will respond.
This is why God has taken hold of us in Christ Jesus.

It is true that we will be completely free from pain, sickness, and this body that decays, and that we will have a glorified body. But that is not all. The day is also coming when we will be completely like Jesus in holiness. We will have no mind of our own. God will only need to show us His will, and right away we will do it.
God is the one who brings about salvation. And this salvation can be received only as a gift of grace.
People cannot help God in the smallest way to bring it about.
Salvation comes completely from God. He gives it as a gift of grace through Jesus Christ, His one and only Son. God wounded Him, bruised Him, and punished Him in our place.
Jesus gave Himself to take our place, and He was punished for us.
“The Lord has laid on Him the wrongdoing of all of us.”
And all that is asked of us is to accept Him, or believe in Him—to accept the salvation He gives us for free.

So suppose someone feels that he is a sinner and asks, “How can I get this precious salvation?” God's Word answers, “Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ” (that is, trust in the Lord Jesus Christ), “and you will be saved.”
We must give no other answer than the one the apostle Paul gave to the jailer at Philippi.

I want to say to you, my dear fellow sinner: Trust in Jesus. Depend on Him. Receive what He has won for you. If you will stop relying on your own good deeds and goodness, and trust completely in Christ, you will be forgiven for your sins this very moment.
The faith in Jesus that receives forgiveness brings you close to God. It takes away the hostility that was between you and God. And it gives peace to your soul.
The first purpose of salvation—the glory of God—is achieved in every sinner who is saved this way.
Now, about the one who has been saved.
God has taken hold of you in Christ Jesus. So in the end you will be made like Christ, and you will be completely happy and holy.
This holiness will show most of all in how perfect your love will be.
God is love, and you will be made perfect in love.
This leads me to a practical point about our meeting today.
We are not yet in heaven, so we are not yet made like God's dear Son. We are not perfect in love now.
But we should aim for this perfect love and seek after it.
We have gathered here now so that our hearts can be drawn together in love.
We are not yet perfect in love. But we should aim for the goal God had in mind when He took hold of us in Christ Jesus.
We should love one another, even though we see weaknesses and failings in one another.
My fellow believers have their failings, and I have mine. God knows all of them, and only He can judge whose are greater.
That is not for us to decide.
Because we believe in Jesus, we share one life. The precious blood of Jesus has bought us. We are God's children by faith, just as surely as we trust in Him to save us.
So we are children of the same Father. We are brothers and sisters in the same heavenly family. Even with our weaknesses, we should love one another and be patient with each other's failings.
But we cannot have fellowship with anyone who lives in sin. And we cannot have fellowship with those who claim to follow Christ but reject the foundations of our most holy faith.
Being loyal to our Lord will force us to keep our distance from such people, even though it hurts.
But out of loyalty to our Head, we are duty-bound to love all true disciples as true disciples. We must be patient with their failings and weaknesses.
Suppose I understand some part of God's truth a little more clearly than my brother does. Is that any reason for me to keep my distance from him?
If I have been taught better, I should use that knowledge not to lift myself up or to praise myself. I should use it for my fellow disciple, and teach him in a kind and loving way.

And if that brother will not accept what I teach, I still must not keep my distance from him. Instead I should pray for him. I should keep being patient with my brother, for the sake of the One who is patient with my weaknesses.
Have I myself been taught everything?
No! A day is coming when I will know, just as I am known.
But that day is not here yet.

I may know a little more than my fellow disciple. Still, I know only in part, and I am what I am by God's grace. If I really do know more—and I may be wrong to think so—that knowledge was given to me so that I could use it to help my brother who is weaker and has been taught less.
If I am strong, let me prove it by putting my shoulder under the load.
The strong should carry the weaknesses of the weak. If I cannot do that, it clearly shows that I am weak myself. Then I have no right to complain about the weaknesses of my fellow believers.
All of us, some more and some less, are still weak and still have much to learn. None of us has any room to boast.
We all owe everything to God's grace. So we should praise Him even more, live more humbly, and try harder to carry one another's burdens.
In just a little while, our blessed Jesus will come again, so that we can be where He is.
Until then, let us love one another.
Love comes from God.
God is love. And whoever loves the most is the most like God.
All the members of the heavenly family should remember the precious blood that bought them. And they should love one another while they are on the way to their Father's house.
I first met Mr. Craik in July 1829.

Several things were true of us both. We were both nearly twenty-four years old then. We had both been to university. At that time we were both studying the Hebrew language with great love and eagerness. We had even both come to know the Lord Jesus at about the same time, while we were at university. But none of these things is what drew me to him. What did draw me to him will become clear in what follows.
In May 1829, soon after I arrived in England, I became very ill.
At that time I had a strong desire to leave this life and be with my Lord, whom I adore. He had loved me and given Himself for me, the great sinner.
But God was pleased to begin to make me well again. I had not expected this, and above all I had not wanted it. To finish my recovery, the doctors advised me to leave London for a change of air.
I went to Teignmouth, submitting to God’s will. In my heart I did not want to live any longer. Still, I thought it was my duty to use this means.
While I was in Teignmouth, I met Mr. Craik. His warm heart toward the Lord drew me to him.
That was what attracted me.
I stayed in Teignmouth only a few weeks, so I did not see much of him. But in January 1830 I went back to Teignmouth, and from then on I lived there.

Now we were drawn together more fully. Between July 1829 and January 1830, I had come to see the main truths about the second coming of our Lord Jesus. I had come to understand that the Holy Scriptures are all we need as our rule, and the Holy Spirit is all we need as our teacher. I had seen clearly the precious teachings about the grace of God. For nearly four years after I was converted, no one had taught me about them. And I had learned about the heavenly calling of the church of Christ, and what that means for the believer’s place in this world.
These same truths filled Mr. Craik’s heart too. So we were soon drawn close together. From then until the day he fell asleep in Jesus, our friendship was close and unbroken for thirty-six years.

The reader will learn from the memoir itself that we kept working in the Word in the same area of Devonshire for about two years and three months. Then, in a very clear way, we were both led to Bristol at the same time. We have worked together there for more than thirty-three years.
People have often said how remarkable it was that we worked together in such harmony for so many years. And this lasted right to the end.
As I write this introduction to help the reader, I want to spend a little time on this point.
It was not because Mr. Craik had no mind of his own and so always gave in to my judgment. Nor was it because I had no judgment of my own and blindly followed him.

All our Christian friends who knew us knew very well that this was not so at all. These were the real reasons. In 1832 I saw that some people liked my dear friend’s preaching more than mine. So I decided, in God’s strength, to rejoice in this instead of envying him.
Like John the Baptist, I said, “A person can receive nothing unless it is given to him from heaven” (John 3:27).
By resisting the devil in this way, I kept our hearts from being divided.
But that was not all.
From that time on, God also greatly honored my preaching of the Word. I mention this only to show that a double blessing came when I resisted the devil.

Then, from the beginning of 1839 onward, the Lord graciously chose to give me great honor. He did this through the Orphan Houses and the other work of the Scriptural Knowledge Institution for Home and Abroad. Now the temptation went the other way. This was especially true as the work grew larger and larger, and God’s blessing on it grew greater and greater.
Now, humanly speaking, it was my dear friend who had reason to be envious.
But what really happened?
Few people, if any, were more truly glad than my friend about all the honor the Lord graciously gave me.
But even that was not all.

One more thing must be added. Whatever spiritual weaknesses my friend or I had, God gave us an honest aim through all thirty-six years of our friendship. We wanted to live for Him and not for ourselves, and to please Him and not ourselves. That is why our friendship stayed unbroken to the end. And this was true even though, humanly speaking, the temptations to grow apart kept increasing instead of decreasing.

We were very different in the way our minds worked and in temperament. Yet we had to work together. Since we first came to Bristol, about 2,500 believers have been received into fellowship. In recent years nearly 1,000 believers have been in fellowship in the church that meets at Bethesda and Salem chapels. We worked among them.
So who can doubt how hard it constantly was to keep on in love and unity? But there was help to be found in God, and we found it to the end.
This is how we parted when I saw my dear friend for the last time.
I kissed him and was about to leave. He was too weak to talk any more, but he said, “Sit down.” He also asked Mrs. Craik to sit down. He wanted to look at us, even though he could not talk.
So I sat there quietly for a while, and then I left.
That was the last time we were together.
The next day I caught a cold and had to stay at home for several days. During that time my dear friend died.
The reader will see from the memoir that Mr. Craik had a very fine mind. But what made him especially lovable to me were these qualities of his character and his spiritual growth:
1. He was very loving.
2. Like Nathanael long ago, he was truly without deceit.
3. He was especially careful to follow his conscience.
Whatever weaknesses or failings he had, you could be sure that he acted according to his conscience.
He did what he did because he believed it was right.

Our views about how certain things should be done were quite different. But I always came back to this: “My friend follows his conscience. If he only saw things as I do, he would surely act differently.”
4. God gave him great mental powers. But he did not use them to make a name for himself or to be admired by people. He used them to shed light on the Holy Scriptures and to explain the truth.

Here is a striking proof of his humility, and of how far he was from seeking honor from people. In 1849 Professor Alexander let him know, on behalf of the University of St Andrews, that they planned to give him a degree. It would be the degree of Doctor of Divinity, or Doctor of Canon and Civil Law.
He politely turned down this honor. Instead he recommended a Christian gentleman who had done much work in biblical studies. He thought the degree might be very useful to that man as an author.

That was done, and this gentleman was given the degree of Doctor of Laws (LL.D.). Some years ago the same university again told Mr. Craik what they had planned and wanted before. And a second time my friend humbly turned down the honor.

This is truly a striking proof. He may have had passing moments when he failed in this. But in his heart he was firmly determined not to seek the honor that comes from people. Instead he wanted to present himself to God as His servant.
5. Mr. Craik showed great sympathy to people who were going through trials and suffering. His loving heart felt deeply for the pain of others.
6. Mr. Craik was above all a man of prayer. He was also a man devoted to studying the Word of God.
He prayed over the Holy Scriptures. He truly dug into the Word as if searching for hidden treasure. He meditated on the Word. I never knew any servant of Christ who did these things more than he did.

The church of Christ as a whole has suffered a loss now that he has been taken away. To all who knew him well, he was a lovely, kind, and truly spiritual Christian. He was also an earnest, devoted preacher of the Lord Jesus. But the main loss is not just that. It is that he was a man who had truly studied the very words of God on his knees, with great care.

I know thousands of believers. But there is no one whose judgment on any part of the truth I would have valued more than that of my friend who has died. This is because he was very careful and prayerful. He worked hard at comparing Scripture with Scripture. He was humble in soul. He knew a great deal of Greek and Hebrew. And he regularly read the Scriptures in their original languages.

About Mr. Craik’s health, I must say this, as someone who knew him so well and for so long. When he was about forty, he looked much healthier than when I first knew him at twenty-four. And this was even more true when he was about fifty.
He was never strong. And like many men with great minds, he was not careful enough to make the best of the health and strength he had.
He usually ate quickly. Even though he had weak digestion, he did not chew his food properly.
Also, when he felt fairly well, he would forget that his body was naturally weak. Then he would work with his mind beyond his strength.

I do not say this to blame that excellent man who is no longer with us. I, his friend, say it as a warning to other believers. For life, health, and strength of body or mind are entrusted to us as precious talents to be used for God.

He did not usually take care of his health, and he overworked his mind. No doubt this sometimes caused a measure of nervous depression. The reader will find signs of this in his diary. It makes Mr. Craik seem almost like a different man from the one people knew in his normal public life. There he was usually very cheerful.
Since I have mentioned his health, I must add this. I am fully convinced that God meant my friend’s natural weakness to be a special blessing to him.

Mr. Craik was a very humble man. It was his sincere and constant desire to use his mental powers for God’s glory. Yet no one could know him well without seeing his natural tendency. He tended to pursue the training of his mind too eagerly and with too much natural love for it. If his body had not been weak, this might have become a great trap for his inner life.
So, to hold him back, the Lord very mercifully gave him this powerful mind together with a weak body. That way he would not give himself too much to developing his mental powers.
I will add one more thing about his health.
I never knew anyone who by nature shrank from suffering as much as he did.
He often talked to me about this.
And yet for nearly seven months before he died, this very man suffered greatly. But he was also greatly upheld in his great suffering.

On Christmas Day 1865, I had more time than usual, so I sat by his bed longer than usual. Suddenly I remembered what he had so often talked to me about. So I told him that now the Lord’s strength was being shown in him, the very man who by nature shrank from pain and suffering.
He saw it and agreed.
And the Lord truly upheld His suffering servant greatly, right to the end.
He went through his sufferings without complaining, even though he prayed and longed to be set free from them.
And at last he was set free.
He fell asleep peacefully, leaning on Jesus.
I, his poor friend who writes this, am still here.
For now the Lord lets me go on serving Him on earth.
Christian reader, please pray that whether this time is long or short, I will be able to spend it truly for God’s honor.
This is why the letter was written. Philemon lived in Colosse. (We can see this clearly from the last chapter of Paul’s letter to the Colossians.
The letter to the church in Colosse was written at the same time as this letter to Philemon.

Onesimus and another brother carried both letters: the one to the church in Colosse and this private one to Philemon.) Philemon, who lived in Colosse, had a slave named Onesimus. While this slave was still ungodly, he ran away from his master Philemon. Then, by God’s providence, as we say, he came to Rome.
At that time Rome was the greatest city in the whole world.
This slave probably said to himself, “If only I could get to Rome! Think of all the chances I would have there.”
He may have thought of this after he left his master.
He travels on from Asia Minor to Rome, full of bright hopes.
“Oh, what pleasures I will enjoy in Rome! What sights I will see in Rome! What friends I will find in Rome!”
No doubt he thought something like this.
And what happened in Rome?
He was converted. This is how God lets people go their own way. He lets them follow the desires of their own hearts. And if they could, they would run farther and farther away from him.
But God says, “You shall go this far, and no farther.”

Many people have gone to London and other places. They did not go there to do good to their souls but to serve the devil. Yet God took hold of them there, in the very way they least expected, and converted them.
Again, Onesimus could have come to Rome and never met Paul.

He could have lived in Rome for fifty years and never met Paul. But God had plans of grace and mercy for him. So in his good providence, God arranged for him to cross paths with Paul. He had to get to know this man Paul.
And who was Paul in Rome at this time?
He was not a great man in the eyes of the world.
In one way he truly was a great man. But in another way he was completely unknown.
At this time Paul was a prisoner because of the gospel.
Paul did not walk around in the marketplace, the Forum, where the great and wealthy people of the capital gathered.
He was in prison, with a soldier guarding him. Yet God arranged things so that this runaway slave had to meet Paul. And Paul became a blessed tool in God’s hands to convert his soul.
This should greatly encourage all of us!

Some of you have loved ones who are far from Christ—fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, and other relatives. Many of them seem to be moving farther and farther from God. They care less and less about the things of God and more and more about the things of this world.
Dear ones in Christ, keep bringing them before the Lord, with faith and patience. One day you will have the joy of finding out that your prayers were not in vain.

We have every reason to believe that Philemon, this slave’s godly master, cared about his spiritual well-being. But when the slave ran away, all seemed lost. Yet God followed him. He took hold of him at the very time when you and I would least have expected him to be brought to the Lord.
Let us read this letter to Philemon and think deeply about it.
Verse 1: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, whom we love dearly and who works with us.”
Paul saw Philemon as someone who worked with him for the gospel.
He speaks of him as a co-worker and treats him that way.

Verse 2: “And to our dear Apphia (Philemon’s wife), and to Archippus, who fights alongside us (this Archippus was a brother who worked hard at preaching and teaching in Colosse), and to the church in your house.”
The house of Archippus was where the church met. In those days people did not build churches and chapels. Instead, believers met in private homes or in places set up for that purpose.
We see an example of this in Acts chapter 20, where Paul was preaching in an upstairs room.
The disciples did not try to have expensive buildings that looked like the temple in Jerusalem.
The first 120 believers met in an upstairs room.
In the same way, the church in Colosse met in Philemon’s house.
Verse 3: “Grace to you.”
Notice how these words come up in the different letters to the churches. There must be a reason for this.
It is not just a common phrase that is added in.
The reason seems to be this. We need to be reminded that God has given us grace through Christ Jesus. And he is willing to give us more and more blessing.
In the same way, we need to be reminded again and again that we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Right now I am speaking only to those who trust in the Lord Jesus Christ. They have passed judgment on themselves. They have condemned themselves before God as guilty sinners. Now they trust in the death of the Lord Jesus Christ, which paid for sin, as the only basis on which God accepts them.

Verses 4–7: “I thank my God, and I always mention you in my prayers. For I hear about your love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints. I pray that the sharing of your faith will become effective as you recognize every good thing that is in you in Christ Jesus.
For your love has given us great joy and comfort, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints.”
This is what the apostle Paul writes about Philemon’s spiritual condition. It is high praise. He was a most blessed man of God. And yet someone says, “He had slaves!”
Yes, he had slaves.
But we must always remember this. Owning slaves at that time did not involve the terrible cruelty of slavery in modern times.
Many of these people worshiped idols, and many things connected with slavery were quite wrong.
Still, generally speaking, we have no reason to believe that there were cruelties like those of slave owners in modern times.

In most places where we read the word “servant,” it means a slave, someone who belonged to a master. But not even once is there a hint of saying, “How wicked you are! How cruel and horrible your conduct is!”

If the love of Christ had moved them to set all their slaves free, the apostles would have been glad. And when these slaves had the chance to become free, they were to accept it thankfully and not turn it down.
The apostle Paul praises Philemon because he was in such a blessed spiritual condition.
He says, “I thank my God.” He says this especially because of verse 5: “I hear about your love and faith.”
This gave Paul reason to praise and thank God in his heart for Philemon.
This is a rather remarkable phrase: “faith and love toward the saints.”
We can understand what it means that he had love. But what does it mean that he had faith toward the saints?
Have you ever thought about this?
It is very important that we try to search out the meaning of what we read in God’s Word.
The meaning is clearly this. He looked at them with faith. He saw that they are God’s children, and he treated them as God’s children.
Whenever we are able to see one another as children of God, and whenever we are able to see Christ in one another, we are showing faith toward one another.
He also prayed that God would help Philemon even more. We should learn from this. Just as Paul prayed for Philemon, we should pray for each other.
This is what he prayed: “that the sharing of your faith will become effective as you recognize every good thing that is in you in Christ Jesus.”

In other words, he is saying: “My dear Philemon, you have received faith, and I pray that you will keep going. I pray that your faith will give you energy and become effective in you. I pray it will give you more and more strength to recognize everything that is good in any of the saints.”
In verse 7 he adds this to his praise: “For your love has given us great joy and comfort, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints.”
What high praise for this dear man!

He was clearly fairly wealthy and prosperous. And Paul says, “We have great joy.” Why? Because Philemon, this blessed man of God, lived such a holy and godly life that the hearts of the saints were refreshed.
Do we, as God’s children, aim for this? Do we try to be a spiritual refreshment to the saints, so that they are refreshed by our godly lives?
This is what we must aim for.

When we give in to our natural tendencies, to our temper, and to other things God hates, we do not strengthen the hands of our fellow disciples. But when we try to do what agrees with the mind of God, we strengthen each other’s hands in God.
When we bring glory to God, we also help other children of God in their life and conduct.
It is just like an army. If one regiment fights well, the other regiments are strengthened. If one regiment turns its back on the enemy, the other regiments are weakened.
It is the same with the Church of God.

Verses 8–14: “So, even though I could be very bold in Christ and order you to do what is right, I would rather appeal to you out of love. I appeal as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

I appeal to you for my son Onesimus. He became my son in the faith while I was in chains. In the past he was of no use to you, but now he is useful both to you and to me. I have sent him back to you. So welcome him, for he is my very own heart. I would have liked to keep him with me. Then he could have served me in your place while I am in chains for the gospel. But I would do nothing without your agreement. I wanted your good deed to be done willingly, not as something you had to do.”
This is a beautiful statement, and it is deeply important.
In short, this is what happened. Onesimus was converted. Paul was a prisoner in chains for the gospel.
What a comfort this good man would have been to him by serving him!
Paul longed to have someone to serve him.
Paul could have said, “This Onesimus is my son in the faith. So I will act as I have a right to act. I will just keep him and let him serve me.”
He could have said, “I am an apostle. I am here in prison for the sake of the gospel. It is right and proper that my child in the faith should serve me.”
Not that way. Not that way.
That was not the mind of Christ. And this blessed man of God tried to act according to the mind of Christ.

He could have said, “I am an old servant of Christ, an old apostle. I have worked harder than any of the others. And since this runaway slave was converted through me, it is only right that I should have him serve me.”
Not that way, because that would be done under pressure.
He would not know whether Philemon was doing it willingly and cheerfully.
He wanted this man of God to do what he did cheerfully and willingly.
Oh, how important it is for us to remember this!
The principle is simply this.

Suppose someone said, “I am in great need. This person is my brother in Christ, and he has plenty of money. He ought to give to me because I am a poor brother. God’s Word requires him to do it, and I have a right to demand it from him.”
Is this the mind of Christ?
It is the mind of the flesh, not the mind of Christ.
You will never find a man of God doing this in the epistles or the gospels.

It is true that if someone has this world’s goods and sees his brother in need but shuts his heart of compassion, the love of God cannot be in him. But on the other hand, it is also true that it is not fitting for a poor brother to insist on it.
The apostle Paul could have insisted on his rights, but he did not.
“In the past he was of no use to you.”
This shows what kind of man Onesimus was: a good-for-nothing, a bad fellow.
Philemon had lost nothing.
“But now he is useful to you and to me.”
Why? Because he was a child of God, a brother in Christ, a member of the body.
This shows us another very important principle.
Every child of God is good for something.
Someone might say, “Here is a very ignorant person who cannot even put two letters together. What good is someone like that to the Church of Christ?”
If nothing else, that person gives others a chance to show grace.
Here is someone who lies helpless in bed year after year.
That person can pray. That person can still show the mind of Christ to anyone who comes to visit.
And suppose none of this were true. Even then, they give those who are healthy and strong the chance to show love to them.
We should always see one another as precious in Christ’s sight.
Our natural tendency is to see the old Adam in one another. We see one another’s failings and shortcomings. The result is misery for one another and dishonor to God.
Oh, dear ones in Christ, let us aim to see Christ in one another.
Onesimus was useful to the greatest of the apostles. Just think of that!
He could not be useless, because he was a member of the body of Christ. And Christ has no member of his body who is completely useless.
“So welcome him, for he is my very own heart.”
Philemon was to welcome him as if Paul himself had come.
And oh, how would Paul have been welcomed?
Philemon would say, “Oh, dear brother Paul, how glad I am to see you here again!” He would throw his arms around Paul’s neck and kiss him many times.
Now Paul says, “Dear Philemon, welcome this runaway slave just as you would welcome me if I came. For he is your brother in Christ, and you will spend a happy eternity with him.”
“But I would do nothing without your agreement.”
But first I must know that this pleases you. I must know that you are satisfied with it and that it is what you wish and want.
How important it is to remember this in our life with God: that we show the mind of Christ.
That blessed One did not try to please himself. Instead, he chose to be the servant of others. In the same way, we must follow the example of that blessed One.
“Perhaps this is why he went away for a while: so that you could receive him forever.” “Forever”—never to be separated again.
This brings us to a precious truth. The disciples of the Lord Jesus are bound together for eternity. They are knit together forever.
And you see, that is so precious.
We may be separated by distance. We may be separated by death. But that is only how it looks.
We are bound together by the bonds of love, not just for this life, but for eternity.
All the poor sinners who rely on the death of the Lord Jesus, which paid for sin, form one holy, happy, blessed family forever. And there will be no separation, ever.
Do we belong to that family?
Do we believe in the Lord Jesus?
How many of us belong to the heavenly family?
How many of us have made up our minds yet?
Ask yourselves this question—you dear young men, you dear girls from the Orphan Houses, and everyone here.
Oh, how blessed it is to belong to the heavenly family!
Oh, how blessed it is to be counted among the members of Christ!
Then let come what may—we are one in Christ, and one in Christ forever!

“He forgives all your sins. He heals all your diseases. He rescues your life from destruction. He crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies. He fills your mouth with good things, so that your youth is made new like the eagle’s.”—Psalm 103:3–5
In this psalm that I read to you, we should notice especially how much the psalmist stresses praise. He says, “Praise the Lord (or Jehovah), my soul, and all that is within me.”
His whole soul is involved in this service.
All of it! The love of his heart and the powers of his mind—all of it!
This is what we should aim for.

It is not that we fail to thank the Lord. I trust that we do. But our thanks should be more spiritual. More and more, our hearts should be involved. All that is within us should be busy praising, adoring, and honoring the Lord.
Then the psalmist adds something remarkable: “Praise his holy name.”
Only believers can really do this.
By nature, we do not care about God’s holiness.
By nature, people like to please themselves. They would like God to be like them.
By nature, holiness is the last thing about God that we care about.
But when we are born again—when we are made new and have spiritual life—a longing for holiness is born in our hearts. And we are glad that God is a holy God.
Then we can look forward to being like him one day.
Only a child of God really cares about admiring God’s holiness and praising him for it.
Then in the second verse the psalmist adds: “Praise Jehovah, my soul, and do not forget all his benefits.”
We are in danger of forgetting God’s mercies.

We are quick to talk about our trials, our difficulties, the loved ones we have lost, and our crosses. But are we just as quick to talk about God’s goodness and admire it? Are we quick to speak of his mercies, shown to us in countless ways every day of our lives?
The psalmist cared about this very much.
Now let us turn to our text:
“He forgives all your sins.”
This is the first blessing the psalmist names.
It is the first mercy he especially wanted to remember.
Notice carefully that out of all the blessings, this one comes first.
And isn’t this the best blessing we have received?
Can any other blessing compare with this one?
Think of all the blessings we have in our business. We should be grateful for them. But what are they compared with the forgiveness of our sins?
Think of all the peace and quiet in our families. We should be grateful for these too. But what are they compared with the forgiveness of our sins?
We should be thankful for good health. But what is a healthy body compared with the forgiveness of our sins?
What is the strength and energy of mind God has blessed us with, compared with the forgiveness of our sins?
It is nothing compared with it.
The psalmist puts this blessing first because it is the best, the greatest, and the most precious blessing a person can have.
Let me ask you lovingly: Have all of us received forgiveness for our sins?
That is the point! That is the point!
Are all of us forgiven sinners?
We are all sinners, every one of us.
Are all of us forgiven sinners?
Have all of us received forgiveness for our sins?
That is the point!
I have no doubt that many hundreds of you here have. But at the same time, I cannot help feeling that many have not.
So this is the all-important question: Which of the two groups do we belong to?

Are we forgiven sinners, whose heavy load of guilt has been taken away? Or are we unforgiven sinners, who cannot look up to God with peace and calm through the atoning sacrifice of the Lord Jesus Christ?
Ask yourself before God: Which group do I belong to?
If I am not forgiven, I have no peace. I cannot look ahead to eternity with peace and calm. And I do not know where my life’s path will end.
It is a terrible thing to go on day after day without being forgiven.
This leads to the question: How can we receive forgiveness for our sins?
Simply by taking hold, through faith, of the atoning sacrifice of the Lord Jesus Christ.
We deserved to be sent to the place of eternal ruin. But God, in his rich grace, did not send us there. Instead, he laid all the punishment for our countless sins on his Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.

God sent him into the world to take our place. There he earned a righteousness for us by keeping the whole law of God. So when poor, guilty sinners trust in him, God sees them as if they had lived the holy and spotless life of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The sinner who believes stands before God in Christ’s righteousness. He hides himself in the righteousness that the Lord Jesus Christ earned for the poor sinner who trusts in him. And God accepts him.
In our place, the Lord Jesus Christ took every bit of the punishment that we wicked, guilty sinners should have suffered.

So God does not expect us to do something to finish the work of salvation. He wants us to accept what he so graciously provides for sinners in his Son. He accepts his Son’s righteousness for the sinner.

But when a sinner believes in the Lord Jesus Christ, a new kind of life begins. He wants to please Christ. He wants his life to make Christ’s teaching look beautiful. He wants to live the way Christ wants.
He does not do this to be saved by it, or to add something to the work of the Lord Jesus Christ.
He has already been saved through faith. He has been forgiven. He has been accepted because of the righteousness the Lord Jesus Christ earned for sinners. And so he wants to please God.
This is the way to be forgiven: simply trust in Jesus, and in this way believe in him.
Everyone who does this is forgiven.
Another important point is knowing that we are forgiven.
We do not have to wait until we die to know this. Much less do we have to wait until the day of judgment.
This blessing is for now. We can know it now. We can enjoy it now.
Someone who does not have it cannot be very happy for long.
This is what brings the peace and joy of the Holy Spirit into our hearts: knowing that our sins are forgiven, even though we are wicked and guilty.
My dear Christian friends, are all of us enjoying the forgiveness of our sins?
I hope no one says it is impossible to have it.
It certainly is possible. The first Christians enjoyed this blessing.
They knew whom they believed. They knew that in him they had “redemption through his blood—that is, the forgiveness of sins.”
They were told this about the Lord Jesus Christ: “All the prophets bear witness to him: through his name, everyone who believes in him will receive forgiveness of sins.”
So every poor sinner who believes in Jesus is forgiven.
This really is a blessing we can have now.
If any of you do not have this blessing, do not give the Lord any rest until you know that your sins are forgiven.
You really can have it and enjoy it now, because salvation brings blessing with it right now.
This is one of the blessings that come with believing in the Lord Jesus Christ: knowing that we are forgiven.
Notice something else in what the psalmist says. He does not say, “He forgives some of your sins.” He says ALL.
That is so precious.
It is not that five hundred of our sins are forgiven, or five thousand. Every single one is forgiven. Even though they cannot be counted, every one is forgiven.
Just think of it! We are vile and guilty. Yet every sin of everyone who believes in the Lord Jesus Christ is forgiven.
Are you enjoying this?
I really do enjoy the forgiveness of my sins.
It is not because I have very strong feelings.
I do not depend on feelings.
I take God at his word.
I depend on his word: “Whoever believes in him will not perish, but will have eternal life.”
I believe in Jesus, so I have been forgiven.
I have not had any dream or vision about it.
Some people think they must stay in doubt unless they see some strange vision—Jesus hanging on the cross in some corner of the room.
I have had no vision like that.
For fifty years I have never doubted for one minute that my sins are forgiven.
I have been a believer all these years. And all this time the word I mentioned, the word I depend on, has been written in the Book. By it I know that my sins are forgiven.
Every believer who is willing to take God at his word has the right to see himself as a pardoned sinner, a forgiven sinner.
It is a blessing, a great blessing, to know that all our sins are forgiven.
Now suppose we had exactly 9,090 sins. And suppose 9,089 of them were forgiven, with just one single sin not forgiven.
What then? That one single sin would bring us to the place of eternal ruin.
Sin is not something to play with.
We must be completely without sin—hidden in the merits of the Lord Jesus Christ and fully forgiven. Otherwise we are unclean, and we cannot come into his presence.
So see how wonderful this statement of the psalmist is: “He forgives ALL your sins.”
All gone! Oh, how wonderful this is!

Every one of them is gone! Sins in what we do, sins in what we say, sins in what we think, sins in what we feel, sins in what we desire, sins in what we intend, sins in what we lean toward—all gone. They are gone as surely as we trust the Lord Jesus Christ to save our souls.
Now I come to a point I especially want to mention. It is to teach Christians, and especially young believers.
We read, “He FORGIVES.”
This shows that forgiveness is something that is going on now.

Christians may say: Sometimes the New Testament speaks as if all our sins were forgiven. At other times it speaks as if we needed to receive forgiveness. And this verse, “He forgives,” sounds as if forgiveness were still going on.
Here is the explanation.

As sinners, we are by nature guilty criminals. In that position, the moment we believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, all our sins are forgiven. As far as our salvation is concerned, this is done once and for all.

But then we leave our old relationship, in which we were guilty criminals before the righteous Judge. We move into the position of children. In this relationship as children, our salvation is settled. Yet we still fail, more or less every day. And whenever we fail and the Holy Spirit makes us aware of it, we must admit it before God with the simple trust of a child. We must tell him that in this way we have not behaved as we should, or that we have left this thing undone, or done that thing wrongly.

With the simple trust of a child, we are to confess to the Lord. Then this word applies: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” And for this the Lord Jesus Christ is needed in his work as High Priest.

As far as our salvation is concerned, when he died he could say, “It is finished.” Then he went up to heaven as the great High Priest. There he still points to the power of his blood on the sinner’s behalf.

It is in this second sense—in our position as children—that we need to confess whenever we go wrong or fail. Then we receive our Father’s forgiveness. And we will receive it just as surely as we confess. I trust this will explain it to my dear Christian friends.
“He heals all your diseases.”
This is the next blessing the psalmist wanted to remember.

We do not mean that diseases of the body are left out. If anyone is cured of a bodily disease, it is not by the doctor’s skill or by the strength of the medicine. It is by God’s blessing on the doctor’s skill.
Still, I believe the main point here is spiritual disease.
You remember what Isaiah said at the beginning of his prophecies: “From the sole of the foot to the head there is nothing healthy—only wounds, bruises, and rotting sores.”
We all know that this was not about the bodies of the Israelites. Their bodies were not in that disgusting state. It was about their spiritual diseases.
This is true of all sinners, at all times, and in all situations.
If we are spiritually pure, it must come from the Lord.

Now here we must especially remember this. The moment a poor sinner trusts in the Lord Jesus Christ, he puts himself into the care of the infinitely wise and gracious Doctor. He does this almost without knowing it.
That blessed One takes him in and puts him into his own hospital, his own infirmary. And he will not let him go until he is completely cured.

And as you all know, no one is ever sent out of that hospital because their disease cannot be cured, as often happens among people. Instead, the patient is cared for until he is completely free from spiritual disease.
The moment we are there, the cure is going on.
This very meeting is meant, with the blessing of Jesus, to help with that cure—to help us out of our diseased state.

And this is what the weakest believer can look forward to. As surely as he believes in Jesus, and as surely as he is not living in sin on purpose, he will finally be brought to the state where he is completely free from sin.
God has taken hold of us so that we will be made like his Son. In the end we will be completely like him, completely holy, and completely free from spiritual disease.
Pride will be gone completely. Irritability, greed, and love for the world will all be gone.
We will be gentle and lovely, pure and holy—just like Jesus.
Oh, what a wonderful future! Jesus will not give up on us until we are completely free from our spiritual diseases.
Then these words will come true: “He heals all your diseases.”
He trains us and cares for us so well that every day something is done toward this complete cure. We should ask ourselves: Have I made some progress today?
Am I a little freer from disease today than I was yesterday?
Am I a little more like Jesus today?

At the new year we should ask: Have I made more progress this past year than the year before? For the Lord’s will for us is that in the end we will be like Jesus. God’s will should only have to be shown to us, and right away, deep in our souls, we should be ready to do it.
The psalmist wanted to be grateful to God for carrying on this cure.
“He rescues your life from destruction.”
This is true in many different ways.
Think about our natural life. If God did not watch over us, what would happen to us?
We are always in danger of losing our lives.
This is especially true of little children.
Look at the dozens of little children near the Tabernacle, with carts and carriages going by. Who can fail to see that God watches over them?
How true this is of our natural life: “He rescues your life from destruction.”
And when we travel, how much danger our lives are in!
Even if we do not travel but lie in our beds, we are always in danger of losing our lives.
How often a stack of chimneys has fallen and crushed people in an instant!
But there is more to it than this.
Our whole life was meant to be lived for God’s glory.
Suppose we had not believed in Jesus—either as the Messiah who was still to come, or as the one who has come. Then this life that was given to us would have been spent in hell.
Our life has truly been rescued from destruction.
But think of those who do not yet believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. Their life was given to them for Christ’s glory and to be enjoyed forever. Yet it could still be spent in hell.
Make sure that your life is rescued from destruction. Unless you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, it is not yet fully true that your life has been rescued from destruction.
There is more. We believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and want to live for him. But suppose we had been left on our own since we believed. We would have fallen away.
It is only because of God’s grace, mercy, and faithfulness that we are on the Lord’s side today and have not gone back into the world.

So how important it is to be grateful that God has held us up! We have his word: “He who began a good work in you will carry it through until the day of Jesus Christ.” And he will never leave us or abandon us.
What a blessed and glorious future this is!
“He crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies.”
This was the next mercy the psalmist especially wanted to be grateful for.
We should clearly understand the picture used here.
Whenever the Bible uses a picture, we should try to understand it clearly. Then we can know what spiritual truth is hidden in it.
The picture here is “crowning.”
We all know that in a country, not a dozen people are crowned, or even half a dozen. Just one person is chosen, and the crown is put on his head as a sign of honor and power.
This one person, chosen and taken out from all the rest, is given this place of honor and power by the crown put on his head.
That is exactly how our heavenly Father treats us who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. We are not one bit better than the worst of people.
We are just as wicked as the poor prisoners on the Cut, or in the Bridewell, or at Lawford’s Gate.
In ourselves we are just as bad as they are—just as bad as the worst people in the city.
When we see drunkards or prisoners being taken away by the police, we should say: If it were not for God’s grace, I would be a drunkard now.
If it were not for God’s grace, I would be in the hands of those policemen.

We should never forget this, right to the end. Then our hearts will be filled more and more with love and gratitude to God, and to the Lord Jesus Christ—more and more, more and more. For if we had been left on our own, we would have been wallowing in sin and in a far worse state.
This is the very point the psalmist has in mind when he says, “He crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies.” “Loving kindness” means grace.
In the Old Testament, in the Hebrew, it means grace.
We owe it to God’s grace and mercy.
If it were not for God’s grace and mercy, we would be like the worst of the worst.
We should remember all this. It will keep us from pride and from thinking we are better than others. And it will keep our hearts filled with love and gratitude to the Lord Jesus Christ.
Now there is one more mercy left that the psalmist wanted to be grateful for.
Precious Lord Jesus Christ, use your servant’s mouth now. By your Spirit, lead your poor servant to bring out the very points that these dear disciples especially need for their help.
Help your servant. Let the word come not only in words but in the power of the Holy Spirit. Then these dear disciples here will not forget it for the rest of their lives.
Your servant asks this for the sake of your dear name.
“He fills your mouth with good things, so that your youth is made new like the eagle’s.”
Notice the picture again: the old eagles shed their feathers. When this has happened, their strength is truly made new, and they become strong and powerful again.
This was true of those who were old.
So the psalmist looked at himself and marveled at what the Lord had done for him.
He is not referring to food, though food is included. We should be very grateful for every crumb of bread and every drop of water, because the food we are given makes our bodies strong and healthy.
The psalmist meant that his mouth was filled with good things, just as the eagle’s was through good food.
But he meant more than this. He was talking about spiritual food, which renewed his spiritual strength.
Now, dear Christian friends, this is the all-important point.
Older believers do not need to become more and more lifeless, careless, and worldly.
As the psalmist grew old, he did not become very worldly. He did not become lifeless, cold, and unspiritual. Instead, his spiritual strength was renewed.
It can be like that for us too.

Some people think that for two or three years after we are converted we may be healthy and lively. Then, after knowing the Lord for five or ten years, we can expect to become cold, dead, and formal, and slowly slide back again. That is a mistake.
It can be very different. It should be very different. And if it is not, we are not living for the praise and glory of God.
In his old age the psalmist was happier in the Lord and more spiritually minded. He had more spiritual power and strength at the end than he had at the beginning.
Oh, my dear younger brothers and sisters, you do not have dull and miserable days ahead of you. You have brighter and happier days ahead.
And here, for the honor and glory of God, I will give my own testimony.

I have been a believer for almost fifty-one years, and I am happier now than I was fifty years ago. I am far happier than I was forty years ago, or thirty years ago, or twenty years ago, or ten years ago.
As time has gone on, my peace and joy and happiness in the Lord have grown more and more, instead of fading away more and more.
Why do I mention this?
Not to boast, because it is all by God’s grace. I say it to encourage my younger fellow believers to expect greater things from the Lord. He loves to give generously.
As you sometimes sing, “More and more, more and more”—there is still more to come.
Let us watch for it, because God loves to give more grace.
It is the joy and delight of his heart to give more and more.
Why shouldn’t it be that way?
Why shouldn’t we have the best things in the last part of our lives?
Has God changed? Not at all!
Has the Bible changed?
No! We have the same blessed word.
Is the power of the Holy Spirit any less?
Far from it. Nothing of the kind!
The Lord Jesus Christ is always ready to bless.
The word we have now is the whole revelation.
And our heavenly Father has the same heart toward his children.
So nothing can stop us from becoming happier as time goes on.
If we are not happier, what is the reason?
There must be a reason. We should ask ourselves why we are not becoming happier and happier.
Now, in brotherly love and affection, I want to give my younger fellow believers a few tips on how to keep their spiritual joy.
If our happiness in the Lord is to continue, it is absolutely necessary to read the Scriptures regularly.
They are the means God has appointed to feed our inner selves.
If you neglect the Word of God, you are not growing. You are spiritual babies, and you stay that way.
And that is not all.
You will become spiritual dwarfs! You will become spiritual dwarfs! Spiritual dwarfs!
Instead of living for God’s glory, you will be living in a way that dishonors him.
You see, after we are converted we are left here to live for the good of the world.
Only a few of God’s children are taken to heaven right after they are converted. The rest are left here for a while to live for God’s glory.
This cannot happen unless we give ourselves to the Word of God regularly—unless we come to it every day and pray over it.
We should think about it and reflect on it in light of our own needs.
But above all, we should read through the Scriptures regularly, in order. We should not pick out a chapter here and there.
If we do that, we stay spiritual dwarfs.
I say this to you with love.
For the first four years after I was converted, I made no progress, because I neglected the Bible.
But when I began to read regularly through the whole Bible, applying it to my own heart and soul, I made progress right away.
Then my peace and joy kept growing more and more.
I have now been doing this for forty-seven years.
I have read through the whole Bible about a hundred times, and I always find it fresh when I start it again.
And so my peace and joy have grown more and more.
So think about this, especially you dear younger brothers and sisters. And say: Let me live for the glory of God.

And if you have reached middle age and have neglected to read God’s Word like this, start now, and be serious about it. Read it with prayer and apply it to your own heart. Try to put into practice what you find. If you do this, your peace and joy will grow more and more, more and more. And it will be said of you, “Your youth is made new like the eagle’s.”
How bright our prospects for eternity are when we take hold of the precious Word!
May the Lord help each of us to do this!
But are there any dear friends here who have not yet been forgiven?

If so, let them now pass judgment on themselves. Let them condemn themselves as guilty sinners. And let them put their whole trust for salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ. Only through him can salvation be found.
When you pray, don’t be like the hypocrites. They love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners, so that people will see them.
Truly I tell you, they have their reward.
But when you pray, go into your own private room and shut the door. Pray to your Father, who is in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you openly.
When you pray, don’t use empty repetitions the way the pagans do. They think they will be heard because they say so much.
So don’t be like them. Your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.
So pray in this way: Our Father who is in heaven, may Your name be honored as holy.
May Your kingdom come. May Your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive those who owe us.
And don’t lead us into temptation, but save us from evil. For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.

For if you forgive others the wrongs they do, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others the wrongs they do, your Father will not forgive your wrongs either.—Matthew 6:5–15.

We will think about part of Matthew 6, starting at verse 5: “When you pray, don’t be like the hypocrites. They love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners, so that people will see them.
Truly I tell you, they have their reward.”
This was really true of quite a few of the Pharisees long ago.

They would stand and pray for a long time in the synagogues. But they did something far worse. The Israelites had a regular time of prayer—about three o’clock in the afternoon by our clock. The Pharisees would plan things so that at exactly that time they were at the street corners. There, as many people as possible, coming from different directions, could watch them pray.
All this was hypocrisy.
In this way they claimed to be very holy men, but in reality the opposite was true.
“Truly I tell you, they have their reward.”
Their reward was the praise of other people.
That is a poor, miserable reward.
“But when you pray, go into your private room.”
The main point here is that prayer should be done in secret.
Not everyone has a little room where they can go and lock the door.
But if it can be done, it should be done.
If it is impossible, God will accept us in the situation and circumstances we are in.
I remember a story I want to tell you. It shows the kinds of situations people may be in.
About fifty years ago I went to Germany to find missionaries for the East Indies.
On this trip I came to Magdeburg. It was one of the strongest and largest fortresses in the kingdom of Prussia.

There, at the home of a godly man in the army, I met a fellow soldier of his. This soldier lived in the barracks. So I asked him, “My dear brother, how do you manage to pray? You are always surrounded by hundreds of soldiers.”
He answered, “When I want to pray in secret, I go down into a large sand cellar. It is completely dark. There I kneel down on the sand.
No one can see that I am there. Often some of the other soldiers come right up behind me, but they never find me there.
I am alone, completely alone. No one sees me. That is my private room.” So God’s children may be in all kinds of different situations, and they have to do the best they can.
But the main point is this: as much as we can, we should try to meet with our heavenly Father in prayer in secret. And we should never try to be noticed by other people so that they will praise us.
“When you pray, go into your private room, and when you have shut your door.” (This shows again how very important it is to pray in secret.)
“Pray to your Father, who is in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you openly.”
Where this happens—where someone waits on God in secret—God will give an open reward in His own time and His own way.
He will show that He is paying attention. He will show that He has written it down in the book of remembrance. He will show that He has not missed it.
“Your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you openly.”
Waiting on God in secret will be made clear by blessing.
If we give ourselves to prayer like this, God will surely notice us. He will give us blessing that anyone can see.
“But when you pray, don’t use empty repetitions the way the pagans do.”

That means repeating the same request, sentence after sentence. The worshipers of Baal did this, and pagan nations still do it today. They think that the more words they use, and the more they repeat what they ask for, the more certain it is that they will get it.
“Don’t use empty repetitions the way the pagans do. They think they will be heard because they say so much. So don’t be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.”
We do not need to pray in order to tell God something. We need to pray simply because God has arranged it this way.

He wants us to come to Him for our own good, profit, and blessing, and to ask Him for the things we need. A blessing given in answer to prayer is so much more precious than a blessing given without prayer.
Very often God allows us to go through great trials. Then, when the blessing finally comes and our prayer is answered, it is all the more precious to us.
“So don’t be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.”
Now comes what is usually called “the Lord’s Prayer.”
“So pray in this way.”
This shows us that God does not intend these words of the Lord Jesus Christ to be the only words we use. Nor does He intend us to use them all the time.
But we should ask for blessing in this spirit, in this way.
That is the lesson we need to learn.
“Pray in this way: ‘Our Father who is in heaven.’”
The very first word is full of meaning.
The requests written here fit God’s children, and only God’s children. They are the prayer of the heavenly family—the people who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
We need to keep this in mind: as long as we do not believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, God is not our Father.
God is God to us.
He is our Creator.
He is the One who keeps us alive.
He is the One who gives us everything we could need.
He lets His sun shine for us. He also lets the rain fall, so that it does us good.
But until we believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, God is not our Father.

Now this word “Our” shows that we are part of a family—part of the heavenly family. Some have been convinced that they are sinners who deserve nothing but punishment. Then they have put their trust in the Lord Jesus Christ to save their souls. All such people—all who believe—have a Father in Almighty God.
“Who is in heaven.”
He is everywhere. But He is especially in heaven, not on earth, even though His power can be seen everywhere and signs of His presence can be found all through the universe.
“May Your name be honored as holy.”
That means: May Your name be honored. May Your name be glorified.
Here I want to remind my dear Christian friends what the word “name” means.
It does not mean the letters that spell the name “God.” It means what we learn in Exodus chapter 34, when Jehovah announced His name to Moses.
It is His character, His qualities, who He is Himself, that should be glorified.
Jehovah should be glorified—the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of all who believe in Jesus.

That is what “May Your name be honored as holy” means. The more we come to understand who God is, the more we find out what a lovely, lovely Being He is—how endlessly lovely He is. “May Your name be honored as holy.”
In other words, “I pray that You will be honored and glorified more and more.”
Now comes another request.

“May Your kingdom come.” That means: “Hurry the time, bring it quickly. Bring the time when You will be honored everywhere and glorified everywhere, when all the works of the evil one will be destroyed.”
This will happen after the Lord Jesus Christ returns.
See how completely impossible it is for ungodly, unconverted people to pray this request from the heart.
Their lips may say it countless times. But its true meaning is nothing less than this: “Let the time come quickly when I, a wicked creature, will be thrown into the bottomless pit.”
That is exactly what the prayer means when they say it. So this clearly shows that ungodly people could only pray “May Your kingdom come” without understanding it.
Only those who believe in the Lord Jesus can use these words in the right way. They beg Him to come back soon, so that God will be glorified and honored everywhere by everyone on earth.
We can see right away from the next words that this is the meaning.
“May Your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.” Since Adam and Eve fell, God’s will has not been done on earth.

It was done in Paradise before Adam and Eve fell. But from the moment they ate the forbidden fruit and the devil brought sin onto the earth, God’s will has not been fully done on earth. It is not done as it should be, and as it will be later, when the Lord Jesus Christ has returned.
Let’s keep this clearly in mind.
One of the first things that happened after the fall was that Cain, the first child of Adam and Eve, murdered his own brother Abel.
There we see the fruit of sin coming into the world. Ever since then, God’s will has not been “done on earth, as it is in heaven.”
At different times there have been people who were godly in spirit. In their own weak way they have tried to glorify God and to live in a way that brings praise, glory, and honor to His name.
But most people on earth have not been doing God’s will the way it is done in heaven.
“Give us today our daily bread.”
Here “daily bread” does not mean just bread and nothing else. It means everything we need for life.
We ask God for what we need, and we are allowed to ask God to give it to us.
Notice carefully that it does not say, “Give us our daily bread,” but “Give us today our daily bread.”
This means we have no right to expect a large supply of earthly things.

God may fill our hearts with reasons to be thankful. He may give us what we need very generously and long in advance. But if He does not, we must not blame Him. Even less should we think He is not keeping His promise. He has not promised to give us what we need years ahead, or months ahead, or weeks ahead, or many days ahead. He has only promised that we will be supplied day by day. And even this is only on the condition that we seek first God’s kingdom and His righteousness.

In other words, suppose we live in the fear of God, and make it our business to win souls for Him and to set a good example of godly living before other people. Then, as surely as we trust Him, we will be given what we need for life.
For this is what David said: “I have been young, and now I am old. Yet I have not seen the righteous abandoned, or his seed”—that is, his children, his descendants—“begging for bread.”
“Give us today our daily bread.”
Under this request we can write clothes, rent, taxes, and everything our family needs.
All of this is included when we ask for daily bread.
And how precious it is to be able to go to a loving Father! It is His great joy and delight to answer what His children ask.
He is not a harsh master or a stern being. He is a Father whose love has no limit.

Oh, how I wish that every one of God’s children would more and more see Him as a Being of endless love! When we come to this point, we are fully satisfied with the way He deals with us, at all times and in every situation.
Whether it is painful or not, we are satisfied that He does all things well.
“And forgive us our debts, as we forgive those who owe us.”
This means admitting that we are sinners.

It is very, very important that we come to God just as we are. We should not try to make out that we are very good, excellent people who always walk in His ways and do what He wants. The very opposite is true, more or less, of every one of us—even the best of us.
So we should more and more admit to God that we are sinners. We have not always acted the way He wants, in every situation. So we have run up debts—spiritual debts—because we are wrongdoers.
We should admit that we are in debt to God. We should ask Him to forgive us for Christ’s sake, looking for forgiveness in the way God has appointed—through Jesus.
We must never try to get forgiveness by pretending that from now on we will live a better life and make up for what we have done wrong. That can never be done.
We can never make up for our past sins. At every moment we are expected to love God with all our heart, with all our strength, with all our might, and to walk in His ways so that His name is praised.
So we can never make up for our past wrongs by what we do.
But through faith in Jesus—if we trust Him to save us—Christ’s righteousness is credited to us.

In other words, the holy work and life of the Lord Jesus is put on our account. It is as if we had been blameless, as if we had been without sin, as if we had lived all our days as faithfully as the precious Jesus did.

His righteousness is credited to us, and only in that way can we be forgiven. We put our trust in Him. We see Him hanging on the cross, shedding His blood as the One who carried our sins. He made atonement for our sins, and only through Him can we be reconciled to God.
“As we forgive those who owe us.”
We need to pay special attention to this.
If someone has offended us, wronged us, or treated us badly, are we ready to forgive?
Do we forgive as a habit?
Even if it happens many times, if the person who offends us and treats us badly confesses it, we must be ready to forgive. And if we do this, then the words apply: “As we forgive those who owe us.”
Here I especially want to say that we have no right to expect answers to our prayers if we are not living this way.
I believe this is very often what keeps our prayers from being answered. We hold on to an unforgiving spirit. We are not ready to forgive those who have offended us and treated us badly.
“Forgive us our debts, as we forgive those who owe us.” That should be true of us.
“And don’t lead us into temptation, but save us from evil.”
As long as we live in this body, we remain weak and helpless, and we are nothing in ourselves. We will be open to temptation and exposed to it.
The Lord Jesus Christ experienced this.
It may be for us as it was for Him: the tempter may leave us for a while.
For a while he may not try hard to overpower us. But it will only be for a while. He will come back.
But that is only one side of the truth. The other side is this: God is ready to come to the aid of His children and help them.
All through their journey in this life, if they just admit their weakness, come to Him, and ask for His help, He is ready to help.

So this should be our prayer: that God, in His rich grace, would let us be tempted no more than is truly needed for the glory of His name. And we pray that through it we will come to know more and more of His power and His love, and how ready He is to act for us.
Then it adds, “But save us from evil.”
This especially means the devil himself: “Save us from the evil one, the wicked one.”
